To build muscle with bodyweight movements, first aim at doing easy variations of an exercise; when you're strong enough for those, then you pick a harder variation of the same type of exercise, over and over. At first progress will be very fast, but as you get stronger it takes more time to make the same amount of progress.

I'd suggest doing these 3 times per week: 1. Pull ups (an easy variation is negative pullups) 2. Handstand pushups (start by learning to do a handstand) 3. Horizontal rows (like pullups, but instead your body is horizontal; start with almost upright rows and gradually decline) 4. Push ups (start with normal pushups; if you can't do them, incline yourself until you can do them) 5. L-sits 6. Pistols (you can start with normal squats)

Find at which variation you can do 6-8 reps, then do 3 sets of each exercise for the amount of reps, with a break of 2 to 5 minutes between sets. When you can do more than 8 reps, move to a harder variation that you can only do for 6 reps.

You'll probably have to google more about these movements.

Your posture looks alright (looks can be deceiving,) I would first work on getting full ROM in the shoulders and spine. How you want to do that is a lecture in itself, but you need to be able to hit arched positions like prone cobra -> archbody hold (superman) and hollow body hold -> hollow body rocks. For the shoulders 0 popping/cracking shoulder dislocates with a weighted bar are a great indicator of shoulder health.

For mass you could:

-Buy a heavy kettlebell, take a course to learn how to swing it, clean it, and jerk it. -Go to a barbell gym and learn to squat and press.

You're gonna want to do some bodyweight work regardless of what you are doing, especially for gaining end range in your joints. But a good kettlebell can take you a long way, and then you can trade/buy a new one after a few months. You really don't need to be adding weight constantly, and after 3 months of using the same weight you can find yourself making a substantial jump in weight.

It's great for if you don't have access to a gym.

If you are training to exclusively meet goals then learn to grow out of that habit. Training to achieve X is a good start but you need to bring your mind to a place where you train purely because you enjoy it. Training to achieve goals will lead you to a point where you burn out and relapse out of training.

In saying this try new ways of training, yoga, body weight training (so much variety here), gymnastics, cross-fit, starting a sport. Just learn something new and learn what your favorites are. Learn well and train safe. As a final point, training should be fun, it won't always be easy, you won't always enjoy doing it but overall you need to train in a way that more often then not leaves you feeling satisfied with what you are doing.

Edit: A toned body will be achieved by having a healthy body fat ratio (about 10% to 16% for guys and about 15% to 20% for ladies, these are estimates). Your muscles will gradually increase in size as long as you continue to challenge and stimulate them. Some forms of trainning induce greater increases in muscles size over others.

Looking more "toned" is simply (not implying it's easy) adding more muscle mass to your frame. Normally, I would suggest lifting weights progressively until you can lift some heavy ass weight. Since that isn't an option for you, bodyweight work is the way to go. Here is a link to a popular BW exercise book:

Thanks. I'll check out that app. Think I should start eating more calories? I don't want to put on more weight and not looked tone. What happens if I do more strength training without increasing calories? And should I focus on aerobic or anaerobic exercise,

At 1200 calories a day, and seeing as you're already pretty lean, I would say to up your intake. Saying that, don't go into complete overhaul. What you're doing got you here, so keep it as a base. Slowly start supplementing your routine with some strength training. Most people would drop their routine to focus on another aspect of fitness that meets their end goal. This is where a lot of people fail. Instead of insanity, maybe you could do a BW workout. If you feel like you're struggling for energy during your workouts, supplement your intake (200-300 calories). Start tweaking, small changes at a time, and you'll begin to notice small differences in your body. When it works, keep it; if you feel like you're getting bulky, cut back on calories.

If you start strength training without increasing calories, you'll probably start "bonking" during your workouts. Basically, you'll run out of energy, and will struggle through the workouts.

Keep aerobic base, add anaerobic lifts.

Looking more tone as Rob said is adding muscle mass onto your body and cutting out the fat deposits. 17.5% BF is a generally healthy frame, but if you're looking to look 'tone' some things you could do to help yourself out:

  • Bulk your chest a bit.

  • If you have the money, buy an adjustable bench. Even something as simple as this..

  • If you have any money left over, get some 20 pound dumbbells. Invest in yourself.

10lb dumbbells are nice, but you're running into the exercise law of progression. At some point your body is simply going to be strong enough that it's not going to feel heavy no matter how many times you do the exercise. Unless you're doing a static hold and even then it becomes easy after a while. You have to get some heavier weights in order to see progression.

  • Tan (CAVEAT) - First things first, part of looking tone is really just real life photoshopping. Getting tan will cause the muscles to pop out that you already have. It also comes with risks of skin cancer, etc. So know yourself before you do that. Spray tans can make you look orange so all of this suggestion do at your own risk.

Electric vehicle batteries are getting cheaper much faster than we expected

This is cool stuff.

The article talks about the EV <-> solar feedback loop. But there is also an EV <-> gas station negative feedback loop. The more people who have EVs, the fewer who stop at gas stations. So the more gas stations close. So the less convenient it is to have a gas burner (as opposed to an EV), so more EVs.

It's not just economies of scale. It's also feedback loops. And those are also going in the right direction.
